biz_vocab.q: Cost per hire is best defined as:
options: Total recruiting spend divided by number of hires
biz_vocab.why: Include internal costs (team, tools, advertising, agency) divided by hires in the period. Quote it with the baseline and the trend.

biz_vocab.q: Time to fill differs from time to hire because:
options: Time to fill counts from requisition approval; time to hire counts from candidate application
Time to hire includes notice period
biz_vocab.why: Time to fill measures the business's wait. Time to hire measures candidate pipeline speed. Interviewers want you to know which one you cite.

options: Offers made divided by interviews held
Offers accepted divided by offers made
biz_vocab.why: A falling acceptance rate points to pay, process speed or employer brand, so be ready to diagnose which.

options: Revenue minus cost of goods or services sold, as a share of revenue
biz_vocab.why: It is what is left after direct delivery costs, before overheads. Hiring affects it through delivery headcount cost and utilisation.

options: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation
Estimated business income, tax, debt and assets
Earnings before income and tax deductions applied
Equity, bonds, income, tax, debt and assets
biz_vocab.why: A proxy for operating profit. Talent cost sits above it, so hiring decisions move EBITDA directly.

biz_vocab.q: Revenue per employee is useful because it shows:
options: How productively headcount converts into revenue
biz_vocab.why: A workforce planning headline: if it falls while headcount grows, hiring is outrunning demand.

biz_vocab.q: Attrition of 20% in a 100-person team means:
options: 20 people left in the period, so roughly 20 backfills
biz_vocab.why: Attrition drives hiring volume. Know what share is regretted loss and what each exit costs to replace.

options: A forecast of roles needed, when, and at what cost, tied to business targets
biz_vocab.why: It converts strategy into hires and budget. Say how you build it: demand forecast, attrition backfill, cost, timing.

biz_vocab.q: Quality of hire is most credibly measured by:
options: Performance, retention and ramp-up speed of hires over time
biz_vocab.why: Combine performance rating, first-year retention and time to productivity. A single number with a method beats an adjective.

options: Does each unit (customer, hire, order) earn more than it costs?
How many units were sold in total?
biz_vocab.why: Apply it to hiring: what does one hire cost, and what does it return? That is the language of a business partner.

lessons.title: Answer in a structure they can follow
lessons.why: The usual failure in senior interviews is not knowledge. It is an answer the interviewer cannot follow, so they say “I'm not following.” A fixed shape fixes that.

steps.title: Headline first
steps.body: Answer the question in one sentence of 25 words or fewer before any detail. If they stop you after that sentence, you have still answered.

steps.title: Three labelled points
steps.body: Say “three things” and number them. Labels let the listener hold the thread while you speak.

steps.title: One example that is yours
steps.body: A real situation with you in it, a number, and a date or scale. One example beats three generic ones.

steps.title: Land on the result
steps.body: End with the outcome in numbers. Then stop talking.

lessons.weak: We did a lot around hiring improvements, working with the team and the business, and it went really well overall, there were many things involved...
lessons.strong: I cut time to hire from 62 to 38 days. Three things drove it: first sourcing, second screening, third manager training. For example, automating screening freed 11 days. The result: 38 days across 120 roles.

fields.label: Headline (one sentence)
fields.hint: Answer the question directly, 25 words or fewer.

lessons.title: Defend every number on your CV
lessons.why: Interviewers pick the biggest number on your CV and pull on it. If you cannot say how it was measured and what the baseline was, the number becomes a liability.

steps.title: Say what it means
steps.body: Define the metric in one line. “Time to hire: days from application to signed offer.”

steps.title: Say how it was measured
steps.body: Name the source and who agreed it. “ATS data, signed off by Finance.”

steps.title: Give the baseline
steps.body: From what to what, over what period. A number without a baseline cannot be judged.

steps.title: Separate your part
steps.body: What you decided and did versus what the team did. Credit the team and keep the credit that is yours.

steps.title: Close on impact
steps.body: Translate it into revenue, cost or margin. “38 days saved roughly $0.4M in vacancy cost.”

lessons.weak: I reduced time to hire significantly across the business.
lessons.strong: Time to hire is days from application to signed offer, from our ATS. I took it from 62 to 38 days over 12 months. I redesigned screening; the team executed sourcing. At our vacancy cost that is about $0.4M a year.

drill.title: Defend one number
drill.prompt: Claim on your CV: “{metric}”. The interviewer says: “What exactly does that number mean?”

fields.label: What it means
fields.hint: Define the metric in one line.

fields.label: Baseline
fields.hint: From what, to what, over how long.

fields.label: What I personally did
fields.hint: I decided... I built... I negotiated...

fields.label: Business impact
fields.hint: Revenue, cost or margin, with a figure.

lessons.title: Say what YOU did
lessons.why: “We” hides your contribution. Interviewers hear it as either a passenger or someone avoiding accountability. Own decisions, share credit for execution.

steps.title: Name the decision
steps.body: What did you choose, and what did you reject? Decisions show seniority.

steps.title: Use I for decisions, we for delivery
steps.body: “I decided to cut agencies to three; the team ran the transition.”

steps.title: Open with a strong verb
steps.body: Led, built, negotiated, redesigned, cut. Avoid “responsible for”, “helped”, “involved in”.

lessons.weak: Responsible for helping the team with the agency process.
lessons.strong: Cut agency suppliers from 14 to 3 and renegotiated fees, saving 31% ($380k a year).

drill.title: Rewrite your own weakest lines
drill.prompt: Rewrite each line with a strong verb, your scope, a number and the result.

lessons.title: Rewrite CV lines as proof
lessons.why: Your CV decides which claims the interviewer attacks. Lines with a number, scope and result invite questions you want. Vague lines invite questions you do not.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Strong verb + what + scope (team, budget, volume) + result with a number.

steps.title: Put the result in the line
steps.body: “Reduced X from A to B by doing C.” If you cannot fill A and B, find them before the interview.

steps.title: Keep it to one breath
steps.body: Under 28 words. Move the story to your answer, not the bullet.

lessons.weak: Worked on improving the hiring process for various teams.
lessons.strong: Redesigned screening for 8 teams, cutting time to hire from 62 to 38 days across 120 roles.

drill.title: Rewrite your weakest lines
drill.prompt: Rewrite each line as proof: verb, scope, number, result. We re-score it instantly.

lessons.title: Speak P&L like an operator
lessons.why: Senior interviews test business thinking. When asked about impact, most talent leaders talk activity. Walk the P&L instead: revenue, cost, margin, people, operations, growth.

steps.title: Revenue
steps.body: How does hiring speed or quality affect revenue? Roles unfilled mean revenue not delivered. Quote revenue per employee or vacancy cost.

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: Cost per hire, agency spend, tooling, and the cost of a vacancy or a bad hire.

steps.title: Margin
steps.body: What your actions did to gross or operating margin: lower cost per hire, better utilisation, less attrition.

steps.title: People
steps.body: Retention, ramp-up time, quality of hire, manager capability.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body: Process and capacity: recruiter productivity, requisitions per recruiter, time to fill.

steps.title: Growth
steps.body: How your function enables growth: new markets, new teams, capability the business lacks.

lessons.weak: Talent acquisition supports the business by finding good people quickly.
lessons.strong: Revenue: unfilled sales roles cost about $60k each per month. Cost: cost per hire fell 24%. Margin: agency savings added roughly 0.4 points to operating margin. People: first-year retention rose to 91%. Operations: each recruiter now handles 22 reqs. Growth: we staffed the new region in one quarter.

drill.title: Walk the P&L for your function
drill.prompt: Question: “How does talent acquisition affect the P&L in your company?” Use your own numbers or sensible estimates.

fields.label: Revenue
fields.hint: Vacancy cost, revenue per employee, delivery capacity.

fields.label: Cost
fields.hint: Cost per hire, agency spend, cost of a bad hire.

fields.label: Margin
fields.hint: Effect on gross or operating margin.

fields.label: Growth
fields.hint: What hiring unlocks for the business.

lessons.title: Business and hiring vocabulary check
lessons.why: Using terms precisely signals fluency. Using them loosely signals the opposite. Ten questions on the language of P&L and talent metrics.

steps.title: How this works
steps.body: Answer each question. You see the reason straight away. Aim for 8 of 10, and use any you miss as the line you rehearse.

lessons.title: Answer strategically, not operationally
lessons.why: “That's operational. Answer strategically.” Strategic answers diagnose before acting and end by measuring. Operational answers jump to the task list.

steps.title: Diagnose
steps.body: What is really going on and why? Name the cause, not the symptom.

steps.title: Analyse
steps.body: What data would you look at? Name two numbers.

steps.title: Recommend
steps.body: One clear recommendation with the trade-off you accepted.

steps.title: Implement
steps.body: Who, what, by when. Keep it to three steps.

steps.title: Measure
steps.body: How you will know it worked: the metric and the target.

lessons.weak: I would post more jobs, use agencies and speed up interviews.
lessons.strong: Diagnosis: slow engineering hiring is a late-stage drop-off, not a sourcing gap. I'd check stage conversion and offer acceptance. I'd recommend a faster panel and a pay review for two roles. Within 6 weeks, target time to hire under 40 days and acceptance above 85%.

drill.title: Answer a strategic question
drill.prompt: Question: “Engineering hiring is too slow and two key roles have been open for four months. What do you do?”

lessons.title: Recover when you are interrupted
lessons.why: “I'm not following” is not a verdict. It is a request for a headline. People who recover calmly are remembered. People who keep talking are not.

steps.title: Stop and breathe
steps.body: Pause for one beat. Silence reads as control.

steps.title: Bridge
steps.body: “Let me give you the headline.” This resets the listener.

steps.title: Headline with a number
steps.body: One sentence, one figure. Then offer the detail: “Happy to go deeper on any of it.”

steps.title: Never defend, re-answer
steps.body: Do not explain why you were unclear. Answer again, shorter.

lessons.weak: Well, what I was trying to say is that there were a lot of moving parts, and basically...
lessons.strong: Let me give you the headline: I cut time to hire from 62 to 38 days. I can go deeper on how.

drill.title: Recover from “I'm not following”
drill.prompt: You gave a long answer about {claim}. The interviewer says: “I'm not following.” Recover.

fields.label: Bridge
fields.hint: Let me give you the headline...

lessons.title: Land it in a minute
lessons.why: Over about 150 words, interviewers stop listening. Cutting is a skill, and the first thing to cut is context.

steps.title: Cut context first
steps.body: They know your company. Start at the problem.

steps.title: One example only
steps.body: Pick the strongest. Offer another if asked.

steps.title: Cut filler
steps.body: Remove “basically”, “you know”, “kind of”, “sort of”. Pause instead.

drill.title: One minute, one paragraph
drill.prompt: Question: “Tell me about {claim}.” Answer in one paragraph of 150 words or fewer.

fields.label: Your answer
fields.hint: Headline, one example, the result. Under 150 words.
